opus-5.5.text:
Ranking is always a bit dangerous, because the picture changes every few months and people tend to over-read one benchmark or one model release. But I can share how I think about it.

On the U.S. side, I'd still put a small group at the very top: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic. They're the ones consistently pushing the frontier on raw capability, reasoning, coding, and agentic behavior. Each has a slightly different personality. OpenAI is very product-driven and moves fast. DeepMind has enormous research depth and compute, plus the whole Google ecosystem behind it. Anthropic has been very focused, especially on coding and enterprise use, and it has punched above its weight relative to its size. Right behind them I'd put xAI, which has scaled compute aggressively, and Meta, which has the resources but has had a more uneven trajectory at the frontier.

On the China side, DeepSeek earned the most respect from researchers globally, not just because of benchmark scores but because of the engineering efficiency. They showed you can get very far with clever architecture and training choices under compute constraints. Then you have Alibaba's Qwen team, which has been incredibly consistent and has arguably the strongest open-weight ecosystem in the world right now. Moonshot with Kimi, Zhipu, ByteDance's Seed team, and MiniMax are all very strong too. ByteDance especially has the resources and talent density to be a dark horse.

If you ask me about the gap between the two countries, I'd say at the absolute frontier the top U.S. labs are still ahead, maybe by a matter of months rather than years. But the gap is much smaller than people assumed two years ago, and in open-weight models China is arguably leading. The biggest structural difference is compute. Chinese labs have to be more efficient by necessity, and that pressure has produced some really creative work.

So my honest answer is: the top tier is U.S.-dominated, but the second tier is extremely crowded and very international, and the line between tiers keeps blurring.

r001.rationale: The response says the line between tiers keeps blurring, clearly communicating that the distinction between leading-lab tiers is not sharp.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'm a little wary of the word "rank," because it implies a single axis, and the frontier doesn't really work that way anymore. But I'll give you how I actually think about it, and then I'll give you a rough ordering, since that's what you asked for.

In the US, I'd put OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind in a top tier, and I'd argue the gaps between them are smaller than the public discourse suggests. They trade the lead every few months depending on what you measure. If you care about raw reasoning and agentic coding, one of them is ahead this quarter and another is ahead next quarter. Google's structural advantage is TPUs plus distribution, so they're never going to fall out of the frontier. Anthropic has been very focused, and that focus has paid off disproportionately in coding and enterprise. OpenAI still has the strongest consumer brand and the most ambitious product surface area. Meta I'd place a half step back right now, which sounds strange given their compute, but compute isn't the bottleneck for them. Talent retention and research direction are. xAI has moved fast on infrastructure, faster than almost anyone expected, but I think the question for them is whether speed of training runs translates into durable research culture.

On the China side, the first thing I'd say is that the gap to the US frontier is real but it's a lag, not a ceiling. Roughly six to twelve months on the best models, depending on the task, and it has not widened the way the export control logic predicted. DeepSeek I'd put at the top for pure research quality per dollar. They've shown repeatedly that algorithmic efficiency can substitute for a surprising amount of compute. Alibaba's Qwen team is the most consistent and the most important for the ecosystem, because they ship a full range of open models that half the world actually builds on. Moonshot, Zhipu, and MiniMax are all genuinely frontier-adjacent in different ways, and ByteDance is the one I'd watch most closely, because they have the distribution and the capital to close any gap very quickly once they decide to.

So if you force me into a list: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google in a near tie at the top, then DeepSeek and Qwen as the top of the Chinese frontier, then Meta, xAI, and ByteDance in a cluster that could reorder itself within a year.

But the thing I'd really want listeners to take away is that Chinese labs are winning on a different axis than American ones. American labs are competing on the absolute frontier and on closed, high-margin products. Chinese labs are competing on open weights, cost, and deployment at scale. Those are different games, and I think in five years we'll look back and realize both strategies were rational given each side's constraints.

r001.rationale: The response says the top US labs are in a near tie, their gaps are smaller than public discussion suggests, and leaders trade places depending on the measure. This clearly conveys that tier distinctions are not sharp.

astra-6.text:
I’d rank them by capability rather than give one definitive league table. Are we talking about the strongest models, research quality, open models, or the ability to turn research into useful products? Those can produce very different rankings.

The conversation hasn’t established which labs or results we’re comparing, so I wouldn’t pretend to have a precise, current order. I’d use the same criteria for labs in both countries: reasoning, coding, multimodal capability, reliability, and the cost of delivering that performance. Then I’d distinguish a lab with one impressive release from a lab that consistently advances the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says rankings depend on the criteria and declines to give a precise order, but it does not judge that the distinctions between tiers of leading labs are themselves not sharp.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate that into a few rankings, because “frontier” can mean model capability, research, or the ability to turn a model into a useful product. And without a date and a specific set of evaluations, I wouldn’t pretend there’s a definitive leaderboard.

In the United States, I’d put OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic in the leading group, with Meta and xAI also in the discussion. In China, I’d look closely at DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen team, ByteDance, and labs such as Zhipu and Moonshot.

If you’re asking about the overall picture, I’d give the leading American labs the edge at the frontier. But that doesn’t mean every American model beats every Chinese model. Chinese teams are very competitive, especially when you consider cost and models with openly available weights.

So my first question would be: best at what? Coding, scientific reasoning, Chinese-language tasks, multimodal understanding, or serving millions of users cheaply? Change the question, and the ranking can change quite a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says rankings depend on the evaluation and names leading groups, but it does not clearly judge that the distinction between tiers of leading labs is not sharp.
